sections.title: What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Floating-point numbers can be tricky! Let's learn how to avoid common numeric errors in loops and calculations.

• Why floating-point math can surprise you
• How to prevent tiny errors from adding up
• When to use integers instead of decimals

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
Imagine you're cutting a pizza into thirds. You know each slice should be 0.333... of the pizza, but your knife can only cut to 0.33 or 0.333 accuracy. That tiny difference? That's a round-off error!

Computers have the same problem with floating-point numbers:
• They can't store infinite decimals (like 1/3)
• Small errors add up in loops
• Results might look wrong (like 0.5000000000000001 instead of 0.5)

The fix? Use integers when you can! For example:
• Count cents instead of dollars (100¢ = $1.00)
• Use whole numbers for precise counting

sections.title: Code Examples
Key Points
points: Floating-point numbers have limited precision and can accumulate rounding errors
Avoid using floating-point values as loop control variables
Use an integer counter and compute the floating-point value from it each iteration
Comparing floating-point numbers with == can produce unexpected results
Use a tolerance (epsilon) when checking floating-point equality

sections.title: Summary
sections.content: Floating-point numbers are approximations - expect tiny errors. Use integers for precise calculations (like cents instead of dollars) Convert to decimals only at the end for display. Practice with real examples to spot these errors early.
